title: LLM Evals
summary: Builds an eval set and scorer for an LLM feature and tracks regressions with each change. Use it so prompt and model changes are measured, not guessed.
description: Changing a prompt without an eval is guessing with extra steps. This skill builds the smallest useful test harness for an LLM feature: a set of real cases, a scorer for each kind of answer, and a report that shows what got better and what got worse.
The agent prefers cheap code checks where an answer can be checked by code, and uses a model as a judge only for qualities that need reading, with the judge itself spot checked against human labels.
useWhen: You change a prompt or switch models and need to know if quality dropped
Bug reports arrive from users and you want each one to become a permanent test
Stakeholders ask how good the feature is and you have only anecdotes
You want a gate in CI that fails when quality falls below a bar
body:
# LLM evals

No change ships without a before and after number on the same cases.

## Steps

1. Define what a good answer means for this feature in one or two sentences, and list the failure types that hurt most: wrong fact, wrong format, refusal, unsafe content, too long.
2. Build the case file (JSONL): id, input, and either an expected value, a rule, or a reference answer. Start with 30 to 50 cases drawn from real logs and bug reports, cover each failure type, and label edge cases. Add every new bug as a case.
3. Score with the cheapest reliable method: exact or regex match, JSON schema validation, a unit test over generated code, or a numeric tolerance. Use an LLM judge only for qualities like helpfulness, with a written rubric of 3 to 5 points and a different model than the one being tested.
4. Validate any judge: hand label 20 cases, compare, and report the agreement rate. Do not trust a judge below about 85 percent agreement.
5. Run each case more than once if outputs vary, and report the pass rate, not a single sample.
6. Store results per run with the prompt version, model name and date. Print a diff against the last run: cases that flipped to fail first, then to pass.
7. Wire a command (`make eval`) and, if wanted, a CI check with a threshold.

## Rules

- Never put eval cases into the prompt as examples; keep them held out.
- Do not average away a critical failure; report those separately.

## Report

Overall pass rate, pass rate per failure type, regressions against the last run with case IDs, and the cost of the run.

example.prompt: Set up evals for our support reply drafter before we switch models.
example.result: Created evals/cases.jsonl with 42 cases from 6 weeks of tickets, scored by 3 regex checks, a policy rule list and a judge with a 4 point rubric (agreement with 20 human labels: 90%). Current model passes 81%. Candidate passes 84% overall but regresses 3 refund cases, listed by ID. Run with: make eval MODEL=candidate.

faq.question: Is an LLM judge reliable enough?
faq.answer: For some qualities, yes, once checked. The skill measures the judge against human labels first and prefers code checks wherever an answer can be verified by code.

faq.question: How many cases do I need?
faq.answer: Thirty to fifty real ones are enough to start and catch big regressions. The set grows as bugs appear, which is the point.

access: Reads your LLM feature code and example logs you point it at
Writes eval cases and a scoring script
Calls a model API from your environment when you run the evals
